questions.q: Why does POST /invoices/:id/send answer 202 Accepted?
questions.explain: 202 means "accepted for processing, not finished". The response carries the delivery id, so the client can show progress without waiting for the provider.
options: Because the e-mail was sent and the invoice was created
The request was recorded and will be carried out later; the client can poll GET /deliveries/:id for the result
Because 200 is not allowed for POST
To tell the client to retry the request

questions.q: Why is the deliveries row inserted in the same transaction as the invoice's change to sending?
questions.explain: This is the outbox pattern. Before it, a deploy that restarted a server between the two steps left invoices "sending" forever. With one transaction, a crash rolls back both.
options: Because PGlite cannot run two transactions
Either both are saved or neither: there is never an invoice marked "sending" with no record that an e-mail is owed, or the other way round
So the e-mail is sent faster
So that the queue can read the row before the commit

questions.q: The in-memory queue already retries and dead-letters jobs. Why does InvoiceHub also keep a ledger table?
questions.explain: The ledger is the truth, the queue is only the executor. After a crash the dispatcher finds the unfinished rows again; nothing depended on the dead process's memory.
options: The queue cannot run jobs concurrently
The in-memory queue lives in one process and is gone when that process dies; the ledger in PostgreSQL survives and says what is still owed
The ledger makes the queue faster
Vitest needs a table to test against

questions.q: A queue delivers "at least once". What gives the customer "exactly one e-mail" anyway?
questions.explain: You cannot prevent a job from running twice (a crash after the send guarantees it sometimes will). You can make the second run harmless. The key has to reach the system that has the side effect, here the provider.
options: Setting attempts: 1 so the job never runs twice
A very long job timeout
An idempotency key per delivery that reaches the provider, which answers a repeated key with the first result instead of sending again
Catching every error in the processor

questions.q: What does deliveries.dedupe_key text not null unique protect against?
questions.explain: The key names the intent: invoice:1, reminder:1:2026-10-05. The database refuses a second row with the same key, and on conflict do nothing turns the second request into "return the existing delivery".
options: Two workers claiming the same row
Two records of the same intent: a double click on "Send", or two servers recording the same day's reminder
The provider sending the e-mail twice
A job that crashes every worker

questions.q: Right after worker A died, worker B's dispatch claimed nothing. Why is that correct?
questions.explain: The lease is a promise: "this row is mine until then". Only when it expires may someone else assume the owner is gone. A minute later, worker B claimed it.
options: Worker B was not started yet
Worker A's lease had not expired; from outside, a slow worker and a dead one look the same, and taking the work early could run it twice at the same time
The row was already marked sent
The dispatcher only runs once per minute

questions.q: InvoiceHub jobs have a 5-second timeout, 4 attempts and backoff between them. Which lease is safe?
questions.explain: If the lease runs out while a live worker is still retrying, a second worker claims the same row and both run it at once. The lease must outlast the longest legitimate run; longer jobs renew it with a heartbeat.
options: 1 second, so crashes are noticed quickly
5 seconds, the same as the timeout
Comfortably more than all attempts with their backoff, such as the 60 seconds used here
No lease: the queue's own retries are enough

questions.q: The queue already stops after 4 failed attempts. Why does the ledger also retire a row after 3 claims?
questions.explain: An out-of-memory crash kills the process before any error handling runs. Without the claim cap, that poison message would take down a worker every time its lease expired, forever.
options: Because 3 is smaller than 4
A message that crashes the whole process never reaches a catch, so the queue never counts an attempt; only the claim counter sees it come back again and again
To make the dispatcher faster
Because claims are cheaper than attempts

questions.q: Which provider answers should the processor retry?
questions.explain: A 503, a 429 or a timeout may go away. A 422 says the request itself is wrong and will fail the same way every time, so the delivery is marked dead at once and a person fixes the address.
options: All of them: the provider might change its mind
503, 429 and timeouts; not 422 "invalid recipient"
Only 422, because the address might be fixed soon
None: retries cause duplicates

questions.q: INV-0004 throws a TypeError in our own rendering code on every attempt. What does the queue do with it?
questions.explain: Only the processor knows what an error means. isPermanent covers the provider's 4xx answers; an unexpected exception is treated as temporary, which costs a few wasted attempts but loses nothing.
options: Marks it dead after the first attempt, because a TypeError is permanent
Retries it until the attempts are used up, then dead-letters it; the queue cannot tell a bug from a temporary failure
Retries it forever
Crashes the worker process

questions.q: With concurrency: 5, a poison job fails 4 times with backoff. What happens to the 12 other deliveries meanwhile?
questions.explain: A job waiting for its next retry does not hold a slot, and a running one holds only one of five. The demo delivered twelve e-mails while delivery 4 kept failing.
options: They wait until the poison job is dead-lettered
They keep flowing through the other slots; the poison job only occupies one slot while it runs
They are dead-lettered too
They are retried as well

questions.q: Why is the worker's concurrency 5 and not 100?
questions.explain: With 100, the provider would answer 429 to most calls, which would turn into retries and even more load. The demo measured at most 5 e-mails at the provider at once.
options: Node.js can only run 5 promises at once
The provider allows 5 e-mails at a time; concurrency is sized for the slowest or strictest thing the jobs call
The database has 5 tables
Higher numbers disable retries

questions.q: The HTTP handler runs inside a correlation context (AsyncLocalStorage). Why is that context gone when the worker runs the job?
questions.explain: AsyncLocalStorage follows one chain of async calls in one process. A durable hop breaks the chain, so the id must be written down with the job (the ledger's correlation_id) and restored on the other side.
options: AsyncLocalStorage is cleared every second
The job runs in a different async flow, started by the dispatcher's timer, and after a crash maybe in a different process
The queue deletes all contexts on purpose
Because the job data was serialized to JSON

questions.q: What does the queue's contextCarriers option do in InvoiceHub?
questions.explain: The dispatcher sets the context from the ledger row just before queue.add(). The carrier's capture stores it in the job's metadata and restore runs the processor inside it.
options: It stores jobs in the database
It captures the correlation id from the current context when a job is added, and restores it around the processor, so log lines in the worker carry it without a parameter
It retries jobs in a different context
It encrypts job data

questions.q: Why does the 08:00 reminder handler only record reminder deliveries instead of sending the e-mails itself?
questions.explain: A handler that sent 500 e-mails itself would need all of those features again. Recording rows takes milliseconds and hands the slow, unreliable part to the machinery built for it.
options: Scheduled handlers cannot make HTTP calls
The pipeline already has retries, leases, concurrency, dead letters and metrics; the handler stays short, and a crash during it loses nothing that was recorded
Because the scheduler has no clock
To make the reminders arrive later

questions.q: The reminder handler builds its dedupe key from ctx.scheduledAt, not from new Date(). Why?
questions.explain: The key should describe which run this is, and that is the time it was due. The current time depends on how late the process was.
options: new Date() is not allowed in handlers
A run that was due at 23:59:59 but starts a few seconds late would otherwise be keyed to the next day, and could run twice for one day or skip one
Because scheduledAt is in local time
Because ctx.scheduledAt is faster to read

questions.q: Two servers each run the scheduler, and both fire at 08:00 on Monday. What stops customers from getting two reminders?
questions.explain: The demo played exactly that: server A created 1, server B created 0. Running the schedule on one instance also works, but then that instance is a single point of failure.
options: The scheduler detects the other server
Both try to record reminder:1:2026-10-05; the unique dedupe key lets only the first insert through
The provider's idempotency key
Nothing: you must run the scheduler on one server only

questions.q: What does for update skip locked in claimDue give you?
questions.explain: Without it, two dispatchers could select the same queued row and both mark it running. With it, the second one simply takes the next free rows.
options: It skips rows that are dead
Several dispatchers can claim at the same time without taking the same row; each skips rows another transaction has locked
It unlocks rows whose lease expired
It makes the query read-only

questions.q: The job carries only { deliveryId }, and the processor loads the invoice itself. Why not put the whole invoice in the job?
questions.explain: A copy in the job goes stale. It also spreads customer data into queue storage, logs and dashboards. Ids in, fresh data loaded inside.
options: Job data must be smaller than 10 bytes
The job may run minutes later, or again after a crash; loading by id gets the current data, such as a corrected address
Invoices cannot be serialized
Because the provider only accepts ids

questions.q: Why does the dead-letter handler call markDead(...).catch(...) instead of void markDead(...)?
questions.explain: The catch logs the failure and moves on. The row stays running, and its lease brings it back later, so nothing is lost.
options: void is a syntax error here
If the database is down, the rejected promise would be unhandled, and Node.js ends the whole process on an unhandled rejection, killing every running delivery
So the delivery is retried at once
Because catch makes the write faster

questions.q: Which pair of numbers best tells operations that deliveries are in trouble?
questions.explain: Dead deliveries need a person. The oldest waiting delivery (the lag) catches stuck or too few workers, even when no error is ever logged.
options: Total e-mails sent and CPU usage
The count of dead deliveries, and the age of the oldest delivery still waiting
The number of workers and the number of tables
The average invoice amount and the number of customers

questions.q: On SIGTERM, in which order should a worker process shut down?
questions.explain: New claims first, running work second, resources last. Leases are the safety net for real crashes, not the plan for a routine deploy: they cost a minute of delay per claimed row.
options: Close the database, then stop the worker
Stop the dispatcher (no new claims), then worker.stop() so running deliveries finish, then close connections
Call kill() at once; the leases will fix everything
Stop the worker first, then keep dispatching until the process exits

questions.q: Why does replay(id) only update rows where status = 'dead', and reset claims to 0?
questions.explain: The key stays delivery-<id>, so if the earlier attempt did reach the provider after all, the replay still does not send a second e-mail.
options: So that it also restarts sent deliveries
A double click in an admin page cannot restart a running delivery, and the replayed delivery gets its full crash budget again
Because dead rows have no invoice
So the idempotency key changes

questions.q: The queue's retry delays come from calculateRetryDelay. What does this print?
questions.explain: The wait doubles from the base, 20 ms, and stops growing at maxDelay. In production leave jitter on so thousands of failed jobs do not retry at the same instant.

questions.q: A provider that honours idempotency keys receives these calls. What does this print?
questions.explain: The same key is replayed. A key that changes per attempt, such as one with an attempt number or a timestamp in it, defeats the whole mechanism: the retry counts as a new e-mail.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 503 and 429 may go away, and undefined (no status: a timeout or a dropped connection) may too. 422 and 400 say the request itself is wrong.
options: [ false, true, false, true, false ]
[ true, true, true, true, false ]
[ false, true, true, true, false ]
[ false, false, false, false, false ]

questions.q: A processor throws on every attempt. What does this print?
questions.explain: attempts: 3 means three tries in total. The dead-letter entry keeps the last error's message as its reason, which is what InvoiceHub copies into the ledger.
options: tries: 3 reason: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'toLocaleString')
tries: 1 reason: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'toLocaleString')
tries: 4 reason: exceeded maximum attempts
tries: 3 reason: undefined

questions.q: This queue carries a correlation id with a context carrier. What does it print?
questions.explain: The id is captured at add() time: job 1 was added while current was req-41, job 2 after it was cleared. When the processors run, both add calls are long done, so only the carrier can bring the id back, and it restores the previous value afterwards.
options:
invoice 1 corr=req-41
invoice 2 corr=undefined
after the jobs: undefined

invoice 1 corr=undefined
invoice 2 corr=undefined
after the jobs: undefined

invoice 1 corr=req-41
invoice 2 corr=req-41
after the jobs: req-41

invoice 1 corr=req-41
invoice 2 corr=undefined
after the jobs: req-41

questions.q: After a delivery, invoice.delivered is published to two handlers, and one of them fails. What does this print?
questions.explain: By default a failing handler does not stop the others, and publishEvent reports how many succeeded and failed. The delivery is already recorded as sent; a failed side effect needs its own retry (a job), not a re-send of the e-mail.
options:
dashboard updated for 7
1 1

dashboard updated for 7
2 0
Error: audit store is down

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1-5 is Monday to Friday, so from Saturday the next run is Monday 5 October at 08:00 UTC, then Tuesday.

questions.q: A reminder run was due at 23:59:59 but started 3 seconds late. What does this print?
questions.explain: The start time belongs to the next day. Keyed by it, Monday's run would count as Tuesday's, and Tuesday's own run would then find its key taken. The time the run was due is the stable choice.

questions.q: This sketch of claimDue works on an array and a clock. What does it print?
questions.explain: At 500, row 1's lease (until 1,000) still holds, so only the queued row 2 is claimed, with a lease until 60,500. At 2,000 row 1's lease has run out: it is claimed a second time, until 62,000. At 70,000 both leases have run out, so both rows are claimed again. Every expired lease means "the owner may be dead", and the claim counter keeps growing, which is what the cap on claims watches.

questions.q: A handler that credits a customer's balance runs twice for the same message, as at-least-once delivery allows. What does this print?
questions.explain: The naive handler credited ₦4,500 twice. The safe one remembers the message id and ignores the repeat. In a real system the handled set is a table with a unique key, written in the same transaction as the credit.

questions.q: Write classify(error) for the processor. error is { status } (status may be missing). Return "retry" for 429, any 5xx and a missing status, and "dead" for every other 4xx. Print the result for the five sample errors.
questions.explain: A missing status means the request never got an answer (a timeout or a dropped connection), which may well work next time. 4xx answers other than 429 say the request is wrong.

questions.q: Write reminderKey(invoiceId, scheduledAt) that returns a dedupe key like reminder:7:2026-10-05, using the UTC date of scheduledAt. Then record keys in a Set for two servers firing Monday's run and one Tuesday run, and print how many keys were new each time.
questions.explain: The Set plays the unique index. toISOString() is always UTC, so the key does not depend on the server's time zone.
questions.expected:
reminder:7:2026-10-05 new
reminder:7:2026-10-05 duplicate
reminder:7:2026-10-06 new

questions.q: Write createProvider() returning { send(key, to), sentCount() }. send returns { id, replayed }: a new id msg_1, msg_2… for a new key, and the first answer with replayed: true for a key it has seen. Simulate a worker that sends, crashes, and a second worker that sends again with the same key, then print the two answers and the count.
questions.explain: The second worker cannot know whether the first one's e-mail went out; the provider can. That is why the key has to travel all the way to the system with the side effect.

questions.q: Write claimDue(rows, now, leaseMs, maxClaims). First mark as dead every running row whose lease expired (lockedUntil < now) and that already has maxClaims claims. Then claim every row that is queued, or running with an expired lease: set it running, add one claim, and set lockedUntil = now + leaseMs. Return the claimed ids. Play four crashed workers, one lease apart, and print what each claimed and the row's final state.
questions.explain: Retiring before claiming is what stops the fourth worker from receiving the poison. The clock is a parameter, so the test runs in microseconds instead of four minutes.
questions.expected:
worker 1 claimed [ 1 ]
worker 2 claimed [ 1 ]
worker 3 claimed [ 1 ]
worker 4 claimed []
{ id: 1, status: 'dead', claims: 3, lockedUntil: 182000 }

questions.q: Write retryDelays(base, maxDelay, retries) that returns the waits before each retry with exponential backoff and no jitter: base, then double each time, never more than maxDelay. Print the delays for base 1000, cap 30000 and 7 retries, separated by spaces.
questions.explain: These are the same numbers the queue's calculateRetryDelay gives for an exponential backoff without jitter. The cap keeps a long outage from producing hour-long waits.

questions.q: Write oldestWaitingSeconds(deliveries, now): the age in whole seconds of the oldest delivery that is queued or running, or 0 when there is none. Print it for the sample, then again after the oldest one is sent.
questions.explain: The sent delivery is older still, but it is not waiting, so it does not count. A lag that keeps growing means the workers are stuck or too few, even when no error is logged.

questions.q: With @zudojs/queue, write a processor for deliver jobs that treats a "permanent" failure (the job's email has no @) by recording the id in dead and returning normally, and otherwise succeeds. Add one good and one bad job with attempts: 3, wait until both are done, and print how many times the processor ran and the queue's deadLettered count.
questions.explain: Returning normally tells the queue the job is finished, so it never spends the other two attempts on an address that will never work. Your own record (here dead, in InvoiceHub the ledger) says what happened.
